name: abstract-factory
intent: Expose one creation contract for each product kind in a coherent family, letting clients switch the selected family at the composition root without naming concrete products or mixing incompatible variants.
problem: A client must construct several related products that collaborate as a matched set, but direct construction spreads family keys and concrete class names through the code. Adding a family then becomes configuration branches plus constructor edits, while mixing products from different families can fail only after incompatible objects interact.
context: Use in object- or interface-based subsystems with two independent axes of change: product kinds (button, slider, connection, command) and product families or variants (dark/light, PostgreSQL/Oracle, AWS/GCP). The family is normally selected once at a composition root, products from one family are intended to collaborate, and clients must compile, test and ship without knowing concrete product types; if products are intentionally mixed or only one kind is created, use a smaller creator instead.
benefits: Isolates concrete classes: product class names appear only inside the concrete factories, so client code is written and tested purely against abstract product interfaces.
Exchanging a product family is a one-line change at the single place where the concrete factory is instantiated or injected, and the whole family switches at once.
Promotes consistency: the factory is the only place that can pair product variants, so mismatched combinations (a Postgres connection with an Oracle command) are impossible to create by accident.
New product families plug in as new concrete factory classes without touching existing factories or clients (open/closed on the family axis).
The creation contract becomes an explicit, mockable dependency: tests inject an in-memory or fake factory that returns test doubles for the whole family.
Supports configuration-driven backends and plugins: the family key is resolved at a composition root and the rest of the code never sees the resolution logic.
tradeoffs: Adding a new product KIND is expensive: the AbstractFactory interface and every concrete factory must be extended at once, so the pattern trades closed-for-extension on the product axis for open/closed on the family axis.
One more layer of indirection and typically one class per product kind per family; for a single product or two, a simple factory function or constructor is shorter and clearer.
The family must stay coherent at runtime; a client that smuggles in a product from another family still compiles, so consistency is an interface convention rather than a compile-time guarantee.
Product construction often needs configuration (connection strings, theme tokens) that the factory must hold; factories acquire state and a lifetime, which complicates ownership across modules.
Diagnostics get one hop harder: a failure may live in the factory selection, the factory implementation, or a product, and stack traces stop naming the product class.

In garbage-collected and dynamic languages the same structure can be expressed as a plain function or object, so the class hierarchy can be pure ceremony (abstract factories are frequently over-built in Python, Ruby or JavaScript).
A factory that returns null (or None) for a product is a silent wrong-family attack: the caller may not check and corrupted state surfaces far from the factory, making debugging harder.

Shared mutable factory state (e.g., a connection pool held by the factory) creates thread-safety risks when one factory instance serves concurrent clients, requiring synchronization or per-request factory instantiation.

participants.responsibility: Declares one creation operation per abstract product kind; it is the only creation interface client code depends on.
Implements the creation operations for exactly one product family and instantiates the matching concrete products; it is the only place that names them.
Declares the interface for one kind of product (button, connection, command) that all family variants must satisfy.
Implements an abstract product for one family; created by the corresponding concrete factory and used only through its abstract interface.
Uses only AbstractFactory and AbstractProduct interfaces, and stays unaware of which family and which concrete classes it is running with.

Resolves the configuration key, environment variable or injected token to the concrete factory instance; it is the single call site where the family is chosen and must never be duplicated in client code.

use_cases: Cross-platform or themable UI toolkits: Qt's QStyleFactory resolves keys such as "windows" and "fusion" to built-in or plugin QStyle implementations that govern a coherent widget look-and-feel; a fuller abstract factory applies the same family key across several product interfaces.

Provider-independent database code: ADO.NET's DbProviderFactory/DbProviderFactories create a matched DbConnection, DbCommand, DbParameter and DbDataAdapter set for a selected provider such as SQL Server or OLE DB.

Parser-provider plugins: JAXP's DocumentBuilderFactory and SAXParserFactory hide implementation classes behind standard factory APIs, allowing the composition root to select a provider while client code uses parser abstractions.

Java's ServiceLoader documentation uses a CodecFactory service with getEncoder and getDecoder operations; the selected provider supplies a coherent codec family while clients depend only on the service interface.
Test infrastructure: an in-memory factory family whose products are fakes, injected in place of the production family so integration tests need no network.
Game and simulation engines: per-biome object families (terrain, props, audio) that must stay aesthetically consistent when a level is loaded.
SaaS multi-tenant applications: per-tenant theme factories so every rendered page uses the tenant's brand colours, fonts and spacing without per-request conditionals.
Document-format parsers: factory per format (PDF, HTML, EPUB) producing matched tokenizer, layout engine and renderer so a viewer can switch formats from a single configuration key.
avoid_when: There is only one product kind: use Factory Method (an overridable creator for one product) or a plain constructor instead of a family interface.
Only one family exists and no second one is planned: hard-code the products behind a simple factory function; add the abstract layer when the second family actually arrives.

A dependency-injection container already binds the implementations: DI is the composition and lifetime mechanism, so register the chosen family there rather than hand-writing a parallel selector and hierarchy.
Products may be freely mixed, or each is configured independently: there is no family constraint for the pattern to enforce, and the interface locks a set that may not be coherent.
The requirement is step-by-step assembly of one complex product: use Builder, which exposes construction phases and returns one finished object instead of a family of products.
Language or domain favors values over objects (pure functions and immutable data): pass creator functions, records of functions, or classes directly instead of an abstract factory object.

The factory instance must be shared across threads without synchronization: each thread may need its own factory copy, or the factory must be stateless (holding no per-request resources), otherwise use thread-local factories or a factory-per-request lifetime.

The product family changes within a single session (e.g., a live theme-switcher): the factory is a poor fit because every existing product object still carries the old family's state; a component re-instantiation strategy is simpler.
anti_patterns: Wrong move: call a full abstract factory for a single product kind; failure: every family pays for a needless interface and class hierarchy with no family-consistency benefit; instead: use Factory Method or a simple creator.

Wrong move: let clients downcast, isinstance-check or compare product classes; failure: concrete families leak into business logic and every new family breaks those checks; instead: put family-specific collaboration behind abstract product operations.

Wrong move: rebuild the family hierarchy on top of a DI container that already selects implementations; failure: two competing composition roots disagree about lifetimes or family choice; instead: let the container own selection and inject one factory only where a real family contract is needed.
Config-key switch statements inside product constructors instead of in the factory, scattering family knowledge back across the product classes.
A factory that returns shared mutable products (one button instance handed to every client), so per-client state is accidentally shared.

Ambient context: determining which family to use from a global flag, thread-local variable or environment variable read inside the factory, so the family is set implicitly and tests cannot control it independently.

Shared mutable factory state: holding per-request resources (connection pools, caches, configuration) in the factory instance and sharing that instance across threads without synchronization, causing data leakage or corruption.

Factory for application services in LOB applications: replacing direct service injection with a factory abstraction increases consumer complexity (one extra dependency per consumer), forces interaction testing with the factory, and violates the Dependency Inversion Principle since the abstraction is not defined in favor of the client — use a proxy or decorator at the composition root instead.

Factory defined in a shared library for its own concrete types: libraries should not dictate which factory interface clients use; clients define the abstract factory interfaces they need, following the DIP's 'clients own the abstract interfaces' principle.

IDisposable on service abstractions: putting disposal responsibility on the abstraction leaks lifetime management into client code and is a DIP violation; dispose products inside the composition root instead.

Wrong move: use Abstract Factory to configure one complex product step by step; failure: callers still manage sequencing and partially built state, while the family interface adds indirection; instead: use Builder for staged construction.
design_principles: Depend on abstractions, not on concretions: clients name only factory and product interfaces (dependency inversion).
Single responsibility: creating a family is its own responsibility, separate from using the products.
Open/closed on the family axis: new families are added as new concrete factories, without editing clients.
Program to an interface, not an implementation: product class names are confined to the concrete factories.
Encapsulate what varies: the varying dimension is the product family, and it is captured in one factory object.
best_practices: Keep the abstract factory small and stable; when product kinds multiply, compose several smaller factories instead of growing one wide interface.
Return abstract product types from the factory and keep concrete types out of client signatures; ownership must be explicit (unique_ptr, IDisposable, Box<dyn>, GC contract).
Decide the family exactly once, at the composition root (main, DI registration, configuration loader) and pass the factory instance in; avoid global factories with setters.
Inside concrete factories, prefer factory methods, prototype cloning or lambdas over new class-per-product logic so the factory does not become a second product hierarchy.
Make the concrete factory's lifetime explicit (typically one instance per family per process, or one per test) so all products in a session come from the same family.
Provide a fake/in-memory factory family for tests so entire application flows can be exercised without the real products.

Test the factory itself: write at least one test that verifies the factory creates a consistent family (e.g., button and slider share the same theme), not just that each product individually is well-formed.

When the factory must hold mutable configuration (connection string, credentials), treat it as a dependency that must be validated before the first product is created; a failing factory should fail fast with a descriptive message.

Prefer manually-coded concrete factories in the composition root over DI-container-based factory delegation, reserving dynamic proxies (TypedFactoryFacility, etc.) only when the number of factory variants makes hand-coding impractical.

Clients define abstract factory interfaces (not the library that holds concrete types): the Dependency Inversion Principle says 'clients own the abstract interfaces', so define IFooFactory in client code, not in the library that defines Foo.
Decompose large factory interfaces into role-specific sub-factories when the number of product kinds grows beyond what is comfortable to maintain; each sub-factory can be injected independently.

Avoid 'Factory Overload' — an explosion of many narrowly-scoped abstract factories each returning one service type — which adds more dependencies to consumers than it removes; prefer proxies, decorators or a richer abstraction instead.
sources: Gamma, Helm, Johnson & Vlissides, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994), Chapter 2 'Abstract Factory (alias Kit)', pp. 87–95. Creational Patterns.
Martin Fowler, 'Inversion of Control Containers and the Dependency Injection', martinfowler.com (2004) — https://martinfowler.com/articles/injection.html
Mark Seemann, 'Placement of Abstract Factories', ploeh blog (2014) — https://blog.ploeh.dk/2014/12/24/Placement-of-Abstract-Factories/
Mark Seemann, 'Implementing an Abstract Factory', ploeh blog (2012) — https://blog.ploeh.dk/2012/03/15/ImplementingAnAbstractFactory/
Mark Seemann, 'Refactoring from Service Locator to Abstract Factory', ploeh blog (2010) — https://blog.ploeh.dk/2010/11/01/RefactoringfromServiceLocatortoAbstractFactory/

related_patterns_notes.factory-method: creates one product through an overridable creator, while Abstract Factory coordinates one creator per product kind so an entire family changes together.
related_patterns_notes.named-constructor: gives one type a readable construction API, while Abstract Factory hides several concrete product types behind a family contract.
related_patterns_notes.virtual-constructor: dispatches one creation operation polymorphically, while Abstract Factory groups multiple such operations and keeps their products compatible.
related_patterns_notes.prototype: clones configured representatives instead of naming concrete constructors, while Abstract Factory selects a family contract and may use prototypes internally.
related_patterns_notes.singleton: controls how many factory instances exist, while Abstract Factory defines what related products a factory can create; they can be combined but are not substitutes.
related_patterns_notes.builder: assembles one complex product through ordered steps, while Abstract Factory returns ready products across several related kinds.
related_patterns_notes.dependency-injection: supplies the chosen factory or products from a composition root, while Abstract Factory is the family-creation contract that DI may wire.
